title: Exploring Multi-Agent AI Governance with CAESAR 3.1 — Live Simulation Teaser
author: Murky-Atmosphere-705
selftext:
I’ve been building a multi-agent AI governance simulator called CAESAR 3.1, and I wanted to share a teaser snippet from a live run. It’s designed to explore how autonomous nodes (representing AI agents) interact under rogue behavior, quorum-based governance, and energy/load constraints.

Here’s a mini taste of the code that runs the node updates and governance checks:

Copy code

\# Node update snippet

for node in nodes:

\# Update rogue probability with drift, contagion, and energy feedback

node.update\_rogue\_prob(alpha=0.05, energy\_feedback=True)

node.apply\_resilience\_noise()

node.update\_energy\_and\_load()

\# Local + regional quorum governance

cesar.apply\_quorum\_sandbox\_local()

cesar.apply\_quorum\_sandbox\_regional()

cesar.apply\_global\_override()

In a recent small-world network run with 10 nodes over 600 steps:

Average Resilience ℛ: 0.948 ✅

Average Rogue Probability: 0.018

Sandboxed Nodes: 10 / 10

Cascades Detected: 0

Every rogue spike was contained, layered governance fired as expected, and the system self-stabilized.

I’m not posting the full code here to avoid overload, but if anyone’s interested, I can share a lightweight version for experimentation or a discussion on architecture choices, like:

Quorum thresholds for layered governance

Archetype evolution (stealth / aggressive / adaptive)

Energy/load feedback affecting rogue drift

I’d love to get thoughts, questions, or ideas for extending this into larger AI governance labs — for example, topology sweeps (small-world vs. scale-free) or more intense adversarial scenarios.
